title: What a promise adds
bodyMd:
Philosophers have long puzzled over why a promise binds. The puzzle is not why it is good to do what one has said one would do — that much follows from ordinary decency — but why the saying itself creates an obligation that did not exist a moment before. The difficulty was once put very sharply: the words of a promise are, in themselves, only sounds, and no rearrangement of sounds can by itself alter what a person owes.

One familiar answer appeals to expectation. To promise, on this view, is to induce another to rely, and the wrong of breaking a promise is the wrong of disappointing a reliance one has deliberately created. The account is attractive because it explains why a promise that nobody heard, or that nobody believed, seems to bind less firmly. But it explains a little too much and a little too little. Too much, because a confident prediction — "the ferry will run tomorrow" — can create reliance just as effectively without binding the person who makes it to anything at all. Too little, because a promise appears to bind even when the promisee, being wealthy and unhurried, has relied on it not in the slightest.

A second answer treats promising as the exercise of a power rather than the causing of an effect. On this view a promise resembles a conveyance: it transfers to the promisee a small piece of authority over the promisor's future conduct, and thereafter it is the promisee, not the promisor, who decides whether the undertaking may be released. The account has the merit of explaining a feature the expectation theory struggles with — that only the promisee can excuse performance, and that a third party's willingness to forgive is simply beside the point.

Yet it too leaves something unexplained. A power must be conferred by some rule, and the rule that makes promising possible is not one any individual promisor has enacted. Those who promise draw on a practice they did not create and cannot unilaterally alter, in order to give their words the force they claim for them. Whatever else a promise is, it is a borrowing.
accessibilityText: A four-paragraph philosophy passage of about 360 words on why a promise creates an obligation. The first paragraph sets out the puzzle: the mere utterance of words seems unable, by itself, to change what a person owes. The second paragraph describes an expectation account, on which promising wrongs by disappointing a reliance the promisor deliberately created, and objects that the account explains too much (a confident prediction also creates reliance without binding the speaker) and too little (a promise binds even a promisee who has not relied at all). The third paragraph describes a rival account on which promising is the exercise of a power, like a conveyance, transferring to the promisee authority over the promisor's future conduct, which explains why only the promisee can release the promisor. The fourth paragraph objects that this account also leaves something unexplained, because the rule conferring the power is a social practice no individual promisor made, and closes with the sentence: whatever else a promise is, it is a borrowing.

provenance.notes: Original prose written for this question bank. The two positions sketched are standard, widely taught philosophical options discussed in general terms; no published article, book, translation or passage was copied, paraphrased or reconstructed, and no author is quoted.
